questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a script policy does and does not do
questions.learningObjective: Explain the boundary of what a script policy controls
questions.stem: Explain, for your translation notes, what a script policy can and cannot do about a flaw in an attribute.

answer.exemplar: A script policy limits which script sources a page may load or run, so it can block an injected script that points at a source the list does not include. It cannot repair the flaw that let the attribute be broken in the first place, because the injected code may be inline and may already be part of the document. The policy therefore reduces what an attacker can achieve after a successful injection, while the missing encoding remains the defect that must be fixed.

questions.explanation: A good answer separates limiting script sources from preventing the injection itself. It should also say that the policy limits impact rather than removing the defect.
questions.hint: Separate limiting sources from preventing the flaw.

answer.exemplar: Body text is delimited by tags, so an injected value must open a new element before the browser will read it as markup. questions.topic: What a same-site cookie setting does and does not stop

questions.stem: Explain, for your notes, what a same site cookie setting stops and what it leaves untouched.

answer.exemplar: A same site setting limits the requests that carry the cookie to those that do not come from another site, so a page on a different origin cannot make the browser attach the cookie to its request. questions.hint: Look at what each request does beyond a plain send.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A scripting flaw in an attribute rather than in text
questions.learningObjective: Write the note that teaches the attribute flaw from the text flaw
questions.stem: Write the note that explains an attribute flaw to a reader who has only worked through the text case.

answer.exemplar: The text case and the attribute case break out in different ways. In text, the value has to open an element before the browser will treat it as markup. In an attribute, the value only has to close the quote that holds it, and it can then add an attribute such as an event handler that runs when the person interacts with the element. The practical consequence for the notes is that a rule written for text leaves the attribute open, so the attribute needs its own handling of the quote character.

questions.explanation: A strong answer describes both break outs in terms of what the attacker must supply. It should close with the rule that follows for the page being described.
questions.hint: Describe the two break outs before the rule.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why an attribute is a separate case from text
questions.learningObjective: Count the values covered by the attribute rule
questions.stem: A page renders 30 caller supplied values. 11 of them go into quoted attributes and 19 go into element text, and only the attribute positions use the separate attribute rule.
questions.explanation: The attribute rule covers the 11 values that sit in quoted attributes, because the other 19 are handled by the ordinary text rule. The separate rule therefore applies in 11 places on the page.
questions.hint: Count only the values in attributes.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a script policy does and does not do
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a policy did not stop an injected handler

stimulus.body: The example page carries a policy that allows scripts only from the application's own folder, and the comment box writes the comment into the page as an attribute without encoding. The tester reported that a value could add an event handler, and that the handler ran without loading any file.

questions.stem: According to the note, why did the policy not stop the handler?

options.text: Because the policy had not finished loading when the handler was triggered
options.misconception: invents a timing failure

options.text: Because the policy applies only to scripts and not to handlers, and handlers are a different kind of script
options.misconception: treats handlers as outside the definition of script

options.text: Because the handler was written into the page by the comment box, so no source list applies to it
Because the browser ignores the policy for pages that contain a form
options.misconception: invents a form exception

questions.explanation: The policy is matched against the source of a script that the page requests, and the handler was written into the page by the comment box. Nothing was requested from a source, so no list could refuse it.
questions.hint: Ask whether any script was requested from a source.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A script policy beside an unencoded write
questions.learningObjective: Give one combined recommendation for a page with both weaknesses
questions.stem: You are asked to give one combined recommendation for a page that has a script policy and an attribute written without encoding.

options.text: Fix the script policy, since a policy is the control that closes the attribute flaw
options.misconception: puts the fix in the wrong control

options.text: Fix both equally, because neither control can be relied on without the other
options.misconception: demands a redundant second fix

options.text: Fix the encoding and remove the policy, since the policy gives a false sense of safety
options.misconception: discards a useful second layer

options.text: Fix the encoding of the attribute, and keep the policy as a second layer on the sources scripts may come from

questions.explanation: The missing encoding is the defect, so that is what the recommendation has to fix. The policy is worth keeping because it limits the reach of any injection that slips through, and it acts on a different route entirely.
questions.hint: Name the defect first, then the layer that remains.
